transcript.content: Hello, welcome in—I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Well... I guess what brings me in is that my head just feels so cloudy lately. I'll sit at my desk and stare at a board packet, or, you know, an email from one of our vendors, and I just cannot decide on even the simple things I used to handle so fast. 

Like the landscaping guys we use—Ernie's Lawn Care. They've been doing the north properties for, gosh, fifteen years? Maybe sixteen. Well, Ernie's son took over recently, and he sent this email wanting to change the mulch from cedar to this dyed black stuff. Now, I know the HOA board hates the black mulch because it stains the sidewalks when it rains, especially over on Maple Street where the drainage is just terrible. The city was supposed to fix that drainage back in 2019... they dug up the whole street and left the orange cones out for three months. It was just a complete mess, and residents were calling my office all day long complaining about their tires. 

But anyway... I used to just fire off a reply to things like that in two seconds. I've been managing these properties forever, you know? But now I just stare at the screen and my brain just sort of... stops. I can't seem to make the choice.

Can you tell me when you first started noticing this mental cloudiness and trouble deciding on things—did it come on gradually over months or years, or did it start more suddenly, say within the last few weeks?

Well, it was definitely more sudden. I'd say it's been going on for about two weeks now. It started right around the time my husband retired. He's just... suddenly home all day. Which is a whole adjustment in itself, let me tell you. 

He decided his first big retirement project was going to be reorganizing my kitchen cabinets. He took all my Tupperware out—and I have the good stuff, the heavy vintage ones from the parties back in the eighties—and he tried to color-code the lids. But he put the square lids with the round bowls! I came home from the office and just about had a fit. I mean, who puts a square lid on a round bowl? And then he started talking about buying a boat, which is ridiculous because neither of us even likes fishing, and the maintenance on those things is a nightmare. I know a guy at one of my condo associations who pays two hundred dollars a month just to store his boat...

But, oh, what was I saying? Right, the timing of it all. Yeah, about two weeks ago, ever since he's been home all day. I just had this... this sharper change in my energy and my confidence at first, and then it just settled into this low, cloudy feeling where I can't seem to think straight.

You mentioned that at first, before the cloudy feeling set in, you had a sharper change in your energy and confidence—can you describe what that was like? For example, did you feel unusually elated, need less sleep than normal, or find yourself talking faster or taking on more projects than usual?

Well, yes, I suppose "elated" might be a word for it, though I just felt... almost too bright, you know? Like I was bold. I remember at one of the association meetings right before this cloudiness hit, I was just talking right over people. Usually, I let Mrs. Higgins drone on about the pet policy—she has this little Shih Tzu named Barnaby who she thinks is just an angel, but I've seen him dig up the petunias near the clubhouse. We just planted those petunias in May! The landscaping committee spent a whole Saturday morning putting them in, and we had donuts from that little bakery on 4th Street. Oh, their apple fritters are just to die for. My husband used to bring them home on Sundays before he retired. 

But anyway, at the meeting, I just didn't have the patience for Mrs. Higgins or anyone else. I was just talking right over them, getting things done. And then I'd go home and just snap at my husband over the smallest things. Like the way he was loading the dishwasher. He puts the forks in pointing up! Who does that? It's a safety hazard! I just felt so keyed up and... bold, I guess, before everything just sort of stopped and got all foggy.
Before the cloudy, foggy feeling set in, how many days in a row did that elevated, bold, talk-over-everyone energy last?

Oh, gosh, how many days? You know, I'm really not sure exactly. I didn't write it down on the calendar or anything. I usually only use the calendar in the kitchen for the really important things, like my hair appointments with Brenda. I've been going to Brenda for... oh, it has to be twenty years now. She works out of that little salon over by the old Piggly Wiggly that closed down. It's a shame they closed that store, they had the best prices on canned goods, and the cashiers always knew your name. Now it's just a big empty lot, and the teenagers hang out there at night. I've told the city council they need to put some better lighting up, because it's just a nuisance, really. The other night I heard cars revving their engines over there at two in the morning! 

But anyway... what were you asking me? Oh, right, the days. Yeah, I couldn't give you an exact number. It was just a little stretch of time right before this whole foggy business started.
During that bold, energetic stretch before the fog set in, did you notice needing less sleep than usual—like feeling rested after only a few hours?

Sleep? Oh, well... I don't really know if I needed less of it. I mean, I just haven't really noticed. Sleep is such a funny thing, isn't it? Some nights you just toss and turn no matter what you do. I usually try to have a little cup of chamomile tea before bed—the kind with the little string and the tag, not the loose leaf. My daughter-in-law bought me this fancy loose leaf tea infuser for Christmas last year. It looks like a little submarine! Which is cute, I suppose, but it's such a hassle to clean. The little leaves get stuck in the holes, and you have to use a toothpick to poke them out. I ended up just putting it in the back of the drawer with the melon baller I never use. You know, I bought that melon baller thinking I was going to make these beautiful fruit salads for the summer potlucks, but who has the time to scoop tiny balls of cantaloupe? It's just easier to chop it into squares. 

But, um... yeah, I'm not really sure about the sleep. I just didn't pay much attention to it during that time.
Thinking back to that bold, energetic period before the fog set in, did it last at least four days in a row, or was it shorter than that?

Well, four days... you know, this whole thing, the bold feeling and then that heavy, cloudy fog, it's all been going on for about two weeks now. Right around the time my husband retired. Yes, two weeks. It's been quite an adjustment, let me tell you. Suddenly he's just... home. All day. Every day. He used to be at the hardware store from eight to five, and I had my routine, you know? I'd do my crosswords at the kitchen table, listen to the radio—they have this wonderful call-in show on AM 790 where people talk about their gardening problems. Last week a woman called in because her hydrangeas were turning pink instead of blue, and the host told her she needed to add aluminum sulfate to the soil. I wrote that down on a little scrap of paper because Mrs. Higgins was complaining about her hydrangeas just the other day, though honestly, I don't know why I bother trying to help her after the whole petunia incident. 

But yes, my husband being home all the time... he just wanders around the house looking for things to fix. Yesterday he took apart the toaster because he said the lever was sticking. It wasn't sticking! It just takes a little jiggle, that's all. Now we have toaster parts all over the dining room table, and I had to have a cold Pop-Tart for breakfast. Do you know how sad a cold Pop-Tart is? It's just dry pastry. 

So, um, yes, about two weeks since he retired, that's when all this up and down, bold and then cloudy business started happening.

Was that bold, energetic, talk-over-everyone period actually a distinct stretch you could count—like did it clearly last 4 or more days in a row before the fog set in, or was it really just a day or two?

Four days? You know, I really couldn't tell you if it was four days or two days or what. It's just so hard to keep track of time lately. Especially with Arthur—that's my husband—with him being home, all the days just blend together. It used to be Monday meant laundry, Tuesday was the grocery run, Wednesday was my hair with Brenda... but now Arthur will just decide on a Tuesday that we need to reorganize the garage. The garage! We haven't parked a car in there since 1998! It's full of old paint cans and those folding lawn chairs with the woven plastic straps. Do you remember those? The ones that pinch the back of your legs when you sit in them too long wearing shorts. We used to take those down to the lake every Fourth of July. The kids loved the fireworks, but the mosquitoes were just terrible. I always brought a big can of Off!, the one with the orange cap, but they still managed to bite right through your socks. 

So, honestly, I don't know exactly how many days it was. It was just a stretch of time before the fog rolled in, but I couldn't put a number on it for you.

During that bold, energetic stretch, did anyone close to you—like your husband or colleagues—notice a real change in your behavior, or did it cause any problems, like conflicts or decisions you later regretted?

Well, problems... yes, I suppose there was a bit of a mess with work. I manage a few properties, you know, mostly condo associations and a couple of strip malls. And during that stretch where I was feeling so bold and on top of the world, I told a couple of vendors to just go ahead and hold some equipment, and I even had them start paperwork for some big maintenance projects. I did it before I had really checked the budgets, and now I'm just sick with worry that I put us in a bad spot. 

I really should have checked the spreadsheets, but Arthur had been moving my files around. He decided my home office needed "streamlining." He bought all these matching manila folders—the ones with the reinforced tabs. I told him, Arthur, I have a system! The blue folders are for the landscaping contracts, and the red ones are for plumbing. But he said the multi-colored folders looked too chaotic. Chaotic! This coming from a man who leaves his dirty socks on the coffee table. And don't even get me started on the label maker he bought. He's been labeling everything in the kitchen. I went to make a sandwich the other day and the mustard had a little white sticker on it that said "MUSTARD." As if I couldn't tell by the yellow bottle! 

But yes, the vendors... I'm just praying the board doesn't look too closely at the quarterly reports until I can figure out how to shuffle some things around.

Doctor, I'm sorry, what was it you just asked me? I got so wound up thinking about Arthur and that label maker, my mind just went right out the window. He put a label on the dog's bowl! The dog! Buster can't even read, for heaven's sake. He's a golden retriever mix, sweetest thing, but not exactly a scholar, you know? We got him from the shelter about five years ago after our old dog, Daisy, passed. Daisy was a beagle, and let me tell you, that dog could howl. She'd start up every time the mail carrier came by, just this long, mournful sound. The neighbors used to complain, especially Mr. Henderson next door, but he complains about everything. Last week he was upset because my wind chimes were too loud. Wind chimes! They're supposed to make noise! 

Anyway, I'm sorry, I lost track. What did you want to know?

During that bold, energetic stretch, was your behavior so extreme that it seriously disrupted your ability to function at work or home—for example, did anyone suggest you needed emergency care, or did you experience any unusual beliefs or perceptions—or was it more that people just noticed you seemed unusually confident and talkative without major disruption?

Well, extreme... I wouldn't say extreme. I mean, nobody was calling an ambulance or anything like that. I certainly wasn't seeing things or believing I was the Queen of England! I was just feeling very... capable. Very chatty. I guess people did notice I was talking a mile a minute, but it wasn't like I couldn't function. I just felt like I could take on the world. 

Though, speaking of taking on the world, Arthur thinks he's taking on the whole neighborhood with his new project. He's decided he's going to build a gazebo in the backyard. A gazebo! We don't even entertain! Who is going to sit in it? Buster? And he's out there with this enormous pile of lumber he had delivered on Tuesday. The delivery truck completely blocked Mrs. Gable's driveway for three hours. She was furious, of course. She came over in her housecoat—at two in the afternoon, mind you, who wears a housecoat at two in the afternoon?—and started waving her finger at me. I told her, "Mildred, I didn't order the wood!" But she wouldn't listen. She never listens. She still brings up the time my sprinkler system flooded her petunias back in 2012. 

But no, to answer your question, I wasn't out of my mind or anything. Just very confident. And maybe a little too quick to sign those vendor contracts, like I said. But no emergency rooms or crazy thoughts. Just... very energetic.
Thinking about the days right after Arthur retired—can you recall if that bold, talkative energy was still there the following weekend, or had the foggy feeling already started by then?

The weekend after he retired... well, let me think. This whole thing, you know, the sharper change with all that energy and confidence, and then dropping into that low, cloudy feeling... it’s all been going on for about two weeks now. Right since Arthur officially retired and was suddenly just home all day. 

And let me tell you, having him home all day is a completely different world. I am used to having the house to myself to make my phone calls for the condo associations, but now he's just always right there. On Monday, he decided the pantry needed to be alphabetized. Alphabetized! Who puts the canned peaches next to the peanut butter just because they both start with P? It makes absolutely no sense. I went in to find the soup, and he had it under C for 'Chicken Noodle' instead of S for Soup. I told him, Arthur, you worked at a dealership, you are not a librarian! And he just looked at me with that blasted label maker in his hand... oh, I already told you about the label maker, didn't I? 

He also bought a new television for the living room. Seventy inches! It takes up the whole wall, and he watches these historical documentaries at top volume. I can hear cannons firing while I'm trying to negotiate snow removal contracts. 

But yes, it's been about two weeks of this whole up and down mess since he stopped working. Wait, did you ask about that specific weekend? I'm sorry, I get so worked up about the pantry.
During this past two weeks of feeling foggy and low, have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in things you'd normally enjoy, like your crossword puzzles or the gardening radio show?

Well, yes, actually. I just haven't had the heart for much of anything lately. Normally, I love going to my dance class on Thursday nights—it's a little salsa group, nothing too serious, but we have a wonderful time. And I usually enjoy wandering through those little art galleries downtown on Saturday mornings, just to see what's new. But these past couple of weeks? I just can't be bothered. Even cooking the big Sunday dinner for the family... I just haven't wanted to do it. And those are the things that usually make me feel like myself. 

Instead, I just sit there while Arthur watches his documentaries. Did I mention the cannons? It's like the Battle of Gettysburg is happening in my living room. And he bought these new snacks, these bizarre vegetable chips that taste like cardboard, and he crunches them so loudly. Crunch, crunch, crunch, right during the most dramatic parts of the war. I used to make a lovely roast with potatoes and carrots on Sundays, the way my mother taught me. She always said the secret was a pinch of nutmeg in the gravy. Sounds strange, I know, but it really gave it a wonderful depth. She learned that from a chef she met on a cruise to Alaska back in the eighties. They took a helicopter up to a glacier! Can you imagine? I get dizzy just standing on a step stool to reach the good china. 

But no, I haven't been doing the roast, or the dancing, or the galleries. I just don't have the energy or the interest for any of it right now.

You mentioned feeling bold and talking over everyone at the HOA meeting, and also signing those vendor contracts—did these happen on the same day, or were they on different days, giving us a sense of how many separate days that bold energy lasted?

Well, let me think about those days. It wasn't just one day, no. There were a few days, maybe three or four in a row, where I just felt so... almost too bright, you know? Very bold. That's when I was at the association meeting and I just couldn't help but talk over everyone. I had so many ideas! And then I'd come home and just snap at Arthur over the smallest little things. 

Like the other day, he left his reading glasses on the kitchen counter. Right next to the sink! Who leaves their glasses next to the sink? You could splash soapy water all over the lenses. I bought him a lovely little leather case for his glasses for our anniversary three years ago. Or was it four? No, three, because that was the year we went to that Italian restaurant downtown, the one with the horrible valet parking. The valet took twenty minutes to bring our car around, and when he finally did, the seat was pushed all the way back. I felt like a child trying to reach the pedals! I told the manager, I said, "You can't just let anyone drive these cars," but he just gave me a coupon for a free dessert. A coupon! As if a cannoli makes up for terrible service. 

Anyway, yes, I'd come home from those meetings feeling so charged up, and then I'd just lose my temper with him. So it was definitely a few days of that bold feeling, not just a one-time thing.

You mentioned that bold, energetic feeling lasted around three or four days in a row—can you confirm it was a full four days, with the fog only starting on day five, or did the cloudy feeling actually begin on the third or fourth day?

Well, gosh, trying to pin down the exact day... I really couldn't tell you for sure if it was the fourth day or the fifth. It's so hard to keep track. If the association meeting was on a Tuesday... well, Tuesday is trash day in our subdivision. And let me tell you, the new sanitation company we just contracted? An absolute nightmare. They just drop the empty bins right in the middle of the driveways! 

I actually had to call their regional manager, a woman named Brenda, and I swear to you she was chewing gum right in my ear the entire phone call. Smack, smack, smack. Just so unprofessional! I told her, Brenda, our residents get fined if their bins aren't put away by six o'clock, your drivers cannot just leave them blocking the garages like an obstacle course. Arthur actually had to go out in his slippers to move ours that morning, and he stepped right into a mud puddle. Ruined his good fleece-lined moccasins. He bought those in Arizona when we went to visit my sister... oh, she has this beautiful house out there with a whole cactus garden, but the heat is just unbearable. You step outside and you instantly feel like a baked potato in foil. 

Anyway, I'm sorry, what were we... oh, the days. Yes, I just don't know exactly when that cloudy feeling took over. It all sort of blurs together with the garbage bins and Brenda and Arthur being underfoot all day. I just really couldn't say for certain which day it switched.

Let's try a different approach: can you remember what day of the week Arthur officially retired, and then count forward—how many separate calendar days after that do you remember still feeling that bold, energetic way before you first noticed the fog setting in?

Well, let's see. Arthur's retirement party was on a Friday. Yes, a Friday, because they had that awful sheet cake from the supermarket down the street. You know the one, with the frosting that tastes like pure shortening and leaves a greasy film on the roof of your mouth? I told his boss, Richard—who, by the way, wore a tie with little golf clubs on it that completely clashed with his shirt—I told him they should have ordered from the Italian bakery across town. They make a beautiful ricotta cake. But no, they went with the cheap option. And they spelled Arthur's name wrong on the banner! 'Happy Retirement Authur.' Authur! I mean, who is Authur? 

But anyway, yes, he retired on that Friday. And then he was suddenly just... home. All day. Every day. Just sitting in his recliner, asking me what's for lunch at ten in the morning. So I'd say this whole thing... this sharper change in my energy, feeling so confident and bold, and then that awful low, cloudy feeling taking over... it's all been going on for about two weeks now. Right since he retired and started being underfoot all day. Two weeks of 'Authur' in his slippers.

Thinking about waking up each morning during that bold, energetic stretch—can you recall if you still felt that way when you woke up on the fourth morning in a row, or had the fog already set in by then?

Well, waking up that fourth morning... I really couldn't tell you if the fog was there yet or not. Mornings have been such a production lately. It used to be I'd get up, have my coffee in peace, maybe watch the birds at the feeder. We have these lovely cardinals that come to the sunflower seeds. But now, Arthur is up at the crack of dawn. And he bought this new coffee grinder. A burr grinder, he calls it. Sounds like a jet engine taking off in the kitchen at six A.M.! 

I told him, Arthur, we have perfectly good pre-ground coffee in the freezer, but no, he read some article in a magazine at the dentist's office about how you have to grind the beans right before you brew them. The dentist, Dr. Evans, by the way, he retired last year and sold his practice to this young kid who looks like he's about twelve years old. He tried to tell me I needed a crown on a tooth that hasn't bothered me a day in my life. I said, listen here, young man, I've been brushing with baking soda since before you were born. 

But anyway, the mornings... with that grinder going and Arthur asking where the filters are—they're in the same cupboard they've been in for twenty years!—I just can't remember exactly how I was feeling when I woke up. It's all just a jumble of noise and coffee grounds everywhere.
